newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economy's fourth-quarter growth revised down slightly.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economy's fourth-quarter growth revised down slightly.

text.p: The U.S. economy expanded a bit less briskly in the final quarter last year than previously thought, the Commerce Department said Friday, but still entered 1997 on a buoyant note.

In a second and final revision of gross domestic product for the three months from October through December, Commerce said national output expanded at a 3.8 percent annual rate during the quarter instead of 3.9 percent as it estimated a month ago.

The final revised figure for fourth-quarter GDP was a tad below forecasts offered by Wall Street economists, who had expected it to be revised up slightly to a 4.0 percent rate of growth instead of down.
GDP measures the value of all goods and services produced by workers and capital within U.S. borders.

The amended fourth-quarter GDP estimate "was more than accounted for by a downward revision to consumer spending on services, primarily to medical care services, reflecting new hospital data for November," Commerce said.

Most economists anticipate that during the first quarter, which ends Monday, GDP growth will slow modestly to around a 3 percent rate of expansion. But an official estimate of first-quarter performance will not be available for another month.
The economy, now in a seventh year of unbroken expansion from the last recession in 1990-91, clearly retained abundant momentum at the end of last year.
Earlier this week, the Federal Reserve nudged up short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point, concerned that demand was so strong it risked firing up potential inflation.

Consumer spending that fuels two-thirds of national economic activity grew at a $39 billion annual rate in the final quarter. That was revised down from a $39.8 billion estimate made a month ago but was far and away above the third quarter's $5.9 billion rate of increase.
The economy had softened slightly in last year's third quarter, growing at a 2.1 percent rate before speeding up in the fourth quarter to begin this year at a robust pace.
A batch of economic data published Thursday confirmed the expansion's durability.

The Labour Department said first-time jobless claims dropped by 4,000 to 310,000 in the week ended March 22 as jobs were plentiful. And the National Association of Realtors said that sales of existing, or previously occupied, homes jumped 9.0 percent last month to a seasonably adjusted annual rate of 4.26 million units.
Corporate profits after taxes fattened in the fourth quarter last year, rising 1.5 percent from the third quarter to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of $408.2 billion.

But another measure of profits -- called profits from current production that is taken before taxes are paid and with the value of inventories included -- showed a $7.1 billion decline to a rate of $654.1 billion.
The department said that partly reflected a levy put on financial institutions by the government in order to build up an insurance fund against potential failures by savings associations.
Commerce said that businesses added to their inventories at a revised rate of $17.3 billion in the fourth quarter instead of $16.4 billion as it previously estimated.
Analysts say inventories remain relatively lean and that production for the purpose of rebuilding stocks will continue to be a positive influence on national GDP in 1997.
Two inflation measures in the GDP report were revised up slightly but still showed a tame pace of price rises.

The implicit price deflator advanced at a 1.5 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter instead of 1.4 percent. The fixed-weights measure of price changes rose 1.9 percent rather than 1.8 percent as previously estimated.
